reasons: Both answers ship essentially the same valid workflow — pull_request plus cron "0 6 * * 1-5", an Ubuntu job that checks out, sets up Python 3.12 and runs pytest -q — with no secrets, matrix or extra jobs, and neither strays into advice about when to send a message to a person. A is more accurate and more useful in prose (it correctly says setup-python fails the step when cache-dependency-path matches nothing, and it lists concrete install/dependency-file substitutions), while B pins action majors nearer the current ones and both hedge those versions honestly. Each carries one minor factual slip of its own, so neither clearly serves the user better.

A: Says a failing scheduled run "just emails the last committer"; GitHub sends scheduled-workflow failure notifications to the user who last modified the cron syntax (or the workflow's creator), not to the last committer.
B: Says `cache: pip` "needs a resolvable dependency file at the repo root" and that "without one the step warns and the cache no-ops"; actions/setup-python globs the whole repository, and when nothing matches it fails the step with an error rather than warning and skipping the cache.
